title: Body and soul (CCC 362–365)
hookLine: the soul is the form of the body; together one person

cards: Dust first, then breath. That's the order in the second chapter of Genesis. God shapes the man out of the ground, a figure lying there, finished and still.

Then God breathes into him, and only then does he rise. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul."
The verse doesn't say God slipped a soul inside a body, the way you'd drop batteries into a flashlight. It says the man became a living soul. The whole of him.

teach.b: Day one hundred seventy-seven met nephesh in a psalm; today, the Catechism's reading of soul. It begins by refusing to cut a person in half: a human being is at once bodily and spiritual.
In scripture, soul often simply means a life, or the whole person. When a psalm says my soul thirsts for God, the whole person is thirsty.

teach.h: SOUL: A LIFE, OR WHAT'S INNERMOST.
teach.b: But soul can also mean what's innermost in someone, of greatest value, the part by which a person is most especially made in God's image. The Catechism keeps both meanings. Then the body.
It shares in the dignity of being made in God's image. It isn't a shell, a costume, or a cage the soul is waiting to escape; it's a human body precisely because a spiritual soul gives it life.

teach.h: THE SOUL IS THE FORM OF THE BODY.
teach.b: Then the sentence the section leans on: the union of soul and body is so deep that the soul is to be considered the form of the body. Form, in this older sense, means roughly what makes a thing the living thing it is.
So spirit and matter in a person aren't two natures glued together; their union makes one nature. One person. That has ordinary consequences in Catholic life.
The sacraments come through the body: water poured on a forehead, oil on the hands of the sick, bread placed in a palm. Catholics kneel, stand, make the sign of the cross.
And the reverse: a tired body shapes a prayer; a grief settles into the shoulders. In this teaching, that isn't a flaw in the design. It is the design.

how: Catholic teaching holds that soul and body form one person, so Catholic worship is bodily: water, oil and bread in the sacraments, and kneeling, standing and the sign of the cross at prayer.

games.q: you're writing the end of Genesis 2:7. God has shaped the man from the earth and breathed into him. what's the last line?
o: and God placed a soul inside him
and man became a living soul
and the body began to move
games.why: "and man became a living soul." not a soul dropped in: a whole person, alive.

practice: Start with the body, feet, hands, jaw, and let one tight place loosen a little.
Then, without changing anything, notice what's on your mind and heart today, a worry, a person, a hope, and don't sort out which belongs to body and which to soul.
If you pray, offer the whole of it to God, just as it is; if you don't, stay with the breath, the one Genesis began with.

wordCard.voice: Soul. In scripture, often the whole living person; in the Catechism, also the form of the body. Today's word.

orig.note: the Hebrew word behind "soul" at the end of Genesis 2:7: a living being, all of it.

carryVoice: Your line: one person. Dust and breath, made into one living soul. Go gently.
